title: Asteroid Classifier Preprint Reports 96% Fewer False Alarms in Simulation, 40% to 75% on Real Data
excerpt: Asteroid classifier pneo selects about 96% fewer non-NEO targets than digest2 in a simulated Rubin-depth test but only about 40% fewer on real NEO Confirmation Page candidates, an unrefereed arXiv preprint reports. The authors say the Bayesian tool could double near-Earth object follow-up capacity
content:
A Bayesian asteroid classifier called pneo selects roughly 96% fewer non-near-Earth objects than the long-serving digest2 tool in a simulated Rubin-depth test, but only about 40% fewer on real candidates from the NEO Confirmation Page, according to an unrefereed arXiv preprint posted this week by Devanshi Singh, Mario Jurić and Željko Ivezić. The gap between those two numbers matters to follow-up observers, because every non-NEO that reaches the queue uses a telescope slot that could have confirmed a real one.

Rubin Observatory is expected to make that queue far busier. A 2024 simulation projected about 129 new objects a night on the NEO Confirmation Page (NEOCP) during Rubin's first year, roughly eight times today's typical 5 to 27, with only 8.3% of them real NEOs. The pneo authors argue that a more selective filter could potentially double effective follow-up capacity in the Rubin era. That is a projection from the preprint, not a measured result.

Simulated Test Cuts 287 False Alarms to 11, but Real Queue Data Show About 40% Fewer

All three comparisons below hold completeness fixed, meaning the share of true NEOs each method keeps is matched; in the simulated test that is the level set by the current NEOCP posting threshold, a digest2 NEO score of 65.

Test dataWhat the preprint reports
Simulated Rubin-depth tracklets96% of pneo's selection is real NEOs versus 48% for digest2; non-NEO selections fall from 287 to 11 at 93.7% completeness
Real NEOCP discovery trackletsSelection is 1.14 times purer; about 40% fewer non-NEOs
Rubin alert stream and Data Preview 2Selection is 1.4 to 1.7 times purer; 50% to 75% fewer non-NEOs on the alert stream

The 96% figure comes from a simulation, not from the real queue. The authors say pneo's advantage grows at Rubin's depth, where faint main-belt and more distant objects are still largely undiscovered, which describes Rubin better than today's NEOCP. They also argue that the real-data gains are conservative, because the Rubin samples were drawn from cataloged objects and the contaminants pneo removes are mostly faint and distant, so the telescope time saved may exceed what the ratios suggest. One detail in the simulated test is worth noting: pneo and digest2 each selected 269 true NEOs, and 267 of those were shared, so the gain did not come from discarding real objects.

digest2 Scores Are Pseudo-Probabilities, While pneo Computes a Posterior Over All Bound Orbits

A single night of observations gives an object's sky position and motion but not its distance or radial velocity. pneo handles that by averaging a model of Solar System small-body populations over every bound orbit consistent with the tracklet, then reports the posterior probability that the object is a NEO, meaning one with a closest approach to the Sun inside 1.3 astronomical units (about 121 million miles).

digest2 reports a score from 0 to 100 that its authors describe as a pseudo-probability that a tracklet belongs to a given orbit class. The Minor Planet Center's tutorial says digest2 is the primary tool for deciding which tracklets are posted to the NEOCP. The difference is not the inputs, since digest2's score also varies with magnitude and sky position. It is the statistics. pneo's authors say their output is the exact posterior under the model, with no tuned scores or separately chosen priors, and that it is calibrated: across 800,000 simulated tracklets it predicted 10,543 NEOs against 10,550 observed.

The paper also changes the picture of what digest2 gets wrong. In the simulation, 213 of digest2's 287 false alarms were objects with closest approaches to the Sun of at least 4.5 astronomical units (about 418 million miles), sitting about 13 to 89 astronomical units from the Sun (about 1.2 billion to 8.3 billion miles). A further 58 were main-belt asteroids. Of pneo's 11 false alarms, 10 were Mars-crossers near the NEO boundary and one was a main-belt asteroid. In other words, much of the gain comes from rejecting distant objects that digest2 mistakes for NEOs.

Rubin Could Add 129 Candidates a Night, and 64 After Self-Recovery Still Leaves 189 NEOs Undetected

The 2024 study, later published in The Astronomical Journal, found that main-belt asteroids not yet discovered would be the primary contaminant of Rubin's NEOCP submissions. Its authors, who include Jurić, proposed an algorithm that predicts whether Rubin will recover a tracklet on its own, so outside observers can skip it. With that algorithm, the list drops to about 64 candidates a night, of which roughly 5 are true NEOs, and about 189 NEOs would be deprioritized yet still go undetected by Rubin by the end of year one.

That is the trade-off any new filter must beat: shed non-NEOs without discarding real ones. A 2025 analysis of NEOCP candidates posted from 2019 to 2024 found that only about half are ultimately confirmed as NEOs, and that roughly 11% remain unconfirmed because follow-up is insufficient, close to 600 cases a year. Combining a digest2-parameter filter with machine learning, that team cut non-NEOs on the page by more than 80% at a cost of about 5.5% of NEO discovery tracklets. Because most follow-up tracklets of misclassified NEOs are later identified correctly, they put the net loss of true NEOs near 1%.

The two approaches are not directly comparable. The Vereš method was tested on archived NEOCP candidates and works from digest2's own output, while pneo recomputes the probability from the tracklet and a population model. The preprint's real-queue gain of about 40% is smaller than the more-than-80% non-NEO reduction in the Vereš analysis, though the two used different data, thresholds and loss measures.

Population Model Predates NEOMOD3, and Authors Are Tied to Rubin's Solar System Work

"Exact" in the preprint means exact under the authors' model, and that model has stated limits. It is derived from the S3M population model, which predicts about 25% more objects than are known at visual magnitudes brighter than 20.5, and whose NEO component has since been superseded by NEOMOD3.

Other stated limits: the original magnitude distribution ends at an absolute magnitude of 25.5, which the authors extend for small objects; objects beyond 100 astronomical units (about 9.3 billion miles) can receive a spurious NEO probability of 1; interstellar objects are out of scope; and the method handles single-night tracklets only.

The authors are also close to the system being improved. Jurić leads Rubin's solar system team at the University of Washington and co-authored the 2024 study that quantified the follow-up problem; Ivezić has directed Rubin's construction since 2022; Singh was listed as an undergraduate at the University of Washington in coverage of a January 2026 paper. That does not undercut the results, but it means independent testing on other surveys' data would carry weight. The code is open source, which makes that possible.

Will the Minor Planet Center Adopt pneo in Place of digest2?

Nothing in the preprint says the Minor Planet Center has adopted pneo. The Minor Planet Center runs the NEOCP and uses digest2 scores to decide which tracklets are posted, and the preprint describes pneo as a tool that could raise follow-up efficiency, with no deployment plan. The 2025 Vereš team also suggested its methods be used in the NEOCP pipeline, so pneo enters a field where an alternative filter is already on the table.

For observers deciding where to point small telescopes, the practical reading is narrower than the simulation headline: expect a real but modest gain on today's queue, a larger one in Rubin's faint-object regime if the alert-stream results hold, and no change until the Minor Planet Center says otherwise. Each avoided main-belt or distant-object chase frees an hour for confirming high-priority objects before they fade.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the NEO Confirmation Page?

It is a Minor Planet Center web listing of newly submitted observations of objects that might be near-Earth objects, kept so follow-up observers can quickly add measurements before the object is lost.

How is pneo different from digest2?

Both use position, motion and brightness. digest2 outputs a pseudo-probability score, while pneo reports a posterior probability computed from a population model and says it is calibrated against simulated NEO counts.

Could pneo really double follow-up capacity?

The authors say it could potentially do so by raising the share of follow-up targets that are real NEOs. Section VII.3 of the paper ties the claim to the simulated purity gain, from 48% to 96%, and assumes the NEO share among targets translates directly into capacity. Gains measured on real data are smaller: a factor of 1.14 on the NEOCP and 1.4 to 1.7 on Rubin detections, though the authors argue those figures understate the benefit.

Does a "posterior probability" mean the odds are exact?

Only within the model. In Bayesian inference, a posterior combines a prior with a likelihood, and the choice of prior is contested, so results depend on the model behind them, which is why the S3M population limits above matter.
